solution:
Option D, transportation.

The chapter lists the means of transportation and communication among tertiary activities from the moment it defines them, and it devotes a section of its own to transportation, describing it as a service or facility through which passengers and freight are carried from one place to another. Its classification diagram of tertiary economic activities carries transportation as one of its branches.

Each of the other three belongs to a different sector. The use of natural resources is what primary activities do: the chapter says some activities are completely dependent on nature and that we obtain natural resources out of such activities. Raw material is what primary activities supply and secondary activities consume. A finished product is the output of a secondary activity, which transforms raw materials into goods.

Option A, Kochi.

Two of the four are not ports at all. The Delhi International Cargo Terminal and the Nagpur Cargo Hub (MIHAAN) are inland AIR cargo facilities; the chapter names the Delhi International Cargo Terminal among places where loading and unloading of goods takes place and observes that such places are located near water transport OR AIRWAYS, which is the category it falls into. Neither city is on the coast, so neither can be a port in the sense of this question.

That leaves Kochi and JNPT, both on the western coast of India. JNPT is a constructed container terminal, whereas Kochi is a sheltered natural harbour, and the chapter names the Kochi Port Trust among its examples.

The chapter's own principle decides it: coastal area locations are favourable for development of ports and harbours, ESPECIALLY BROKEN COASTLINES, and therefore not all coastal areas can be good ports. A natural port is one where the coast itself provides the shelter, without its having to be built.

Option A, Perth - Sydney.

The answer follows from the name and from geography rather than from any statement in the chapter. A railway runs on land, so a Trans-Australian Railway must begin and end in Australia. Of the four options only Perth - Sydney names two Australian cities: Vladivostok is in Russia and Vancouver in Canada, so options B, C and D each require a railway to cross an ocean, which is impossible.

Perth lies on the western coast of Australia and Sydney on the eastern, so the line named crosses the continent, which is what 'Trans-Australian' means.

[Note: the Trans-Australian Railway appears nowhere in this chapter except in this exercise question. The chapter discusses railways only in general terms, as one of the land means of transport whose construction is easier where relief is not rugged. The key above is therefore derived from the option set and from the meaning of the name, not from the chapter's prose.]
